XML in the real ADDS format for ids= or bbox= queries; stations come from the app's own Scripts/stations.js, values (temp, dewpoint, wind/gusts, sky layers, wx, altimeter, raw_text) from the weather model.
GeoJSON FeatureCollection: Wind Advisory, Flood Watch and High Surf Advisory for CAZ043 timed relative to today; other zones return no alerts.

Nearby-airport list for San Diego; sunrise/sunset computed with the NOAA solar algorithm and moon phases from the synodic month. Placeholder apiKey from the source is ignored.
San Diego Bay / La Jolla stations; hi/lo predictions from a harmonic (M2,S2,K1,O1) tide curve.
Reporting-area forecast JSON for 'San Diego County Region' (AQI 21-58 across days); Open-Meteo hourly us_aqi fallback.
Zone PZZ750 select page and coastal-waters forecast HTML with a Small Craft Advisory banner.
Apache-style directory listings of 5-minute n0r frames and generated palette PNGs (real IEM geometry) rendering the storm's echoes at each frame time.

app.notes: WeatherStar 4000+ is a static jQuery/canvas front end (index.html hosting twc3.html in an iframe) whose only backend is an ASP.NET CORS proxy to NWS/NOAA and other weather services. start.sh runs .ui-capture/stub/server.js (node pinned in mise.toml) on $PORT, serving the repo as-is and stubbing every upstream through the app's own /cors/?u= endpoint. One app source change: Scripts/twc3.js guards the play and music timers (NavigatePlayToggle, AudioPlayToggle) against _WeatherParameters still being null. index.js starts those timers when the iframe loads, before twc3.js finishes its 250ms setTimeout init, which threw "Cannot read properties of null (reading Progress)" on the first ticks. Otherwise the server only injects one <script> (stub/shim.js) after jQuery. Data: all services render one consistent synthetic weather world generated from the current date: a late-season Pacific storm comes ashore over Southern California tonight (showers likely today, heavy rain tonight, clearing Thursday), then tracks over the Four Corners, Plains, Midwest and Great Lakes during the week, with lake-effect showers in upstate NY, Florida showers and PNW showers later. Established-user state: on first visit the shim seeds localStorage the way index.js does after a user picks a location: saved query 'San Diego, California, USA' with its coordinates, English units, Classic theme, auto-refresh on, auto-play on, music muted, narration off, hazard scroll on, plus a saved custom scroll text and RSS URL (not selected). The app opens straight into San Diego (station KSAN, zone CAZ043, radar NKX, ZIP 92101) and cycles through Current Conditions, Latest Observations, Travel Forecast, Regional Forecast/Observations, Local Forecast, Extended Forecast, Almanac/Tides/Outlook, Air Quality, Marine Forecast, Local Radar and Hazardous Weather (3 active alerts). The menu button opens the segment menu; the controls below the TV set location, units, themes, scroll text and auto refresh. Searching another city works through the stubbed geocoder (weather is generated for any lat/lon). Verification: twc3.html run under jsdom with faked canvas (all 12 Progress segments reach Loaded, no uncaught errors including when play/music are toggled before init); a real Chromium could not run inside this sandbox.

This is a checkout of vbguyny/ws4kp (https://github.com/vbguyny/ws4kp) at commit bb6a9aee9485. WeatherStar 4000+

I want to see its user interface in a desktop browser, in the state a real, established user would see it. Please get the app running locally with its main interface working and realistic data in it.

# Running it
- Follow the repo's own setup docs and tooling. Take the simplest route that shows the real app: a static production build if the front end works without a backend, otherwise the app's own server (production or dev mode).
- If it needs a database or other services, run them locally with an embedded or file-based option (SQLite, in-memory, JSON files, an embedded Postgres such as PGlite) or the app's demo/mock mode.
- Don't redesign or restyle anything. Change only what's needed to build and run it.

# Tools: use mise
Install every runtime and tool you need (node, the package manager, python, bun, ...) with mise, pinned to exact versions in a mise.toml at the repo root, so the setup can be reproduced. Match what the repo asks for (engines, .nvmrc, .tool-versions, packageManager). mise is already configured for this directory: `mise install` installs into ./.ui-capture/mise, and its shims come first on PATH, so `node`, `pnpm` and the rest resolve to the pinned versions. Don't use other copies of these tools or download runtimes by hand.

# Secrets, API keys and external services: fake them
The app must not depend on anything outside this machine, and when it runs it has no network except localhost. Wherever it expects secrets, environment variables, API keys or third-party services (hosted auth or OAuth, payment providers, email, LLM or other AI APIs, maps, storage buckets, analytics, hosted databases):
- Give the required variables placeholder values so the app starts.
- Where it actually calls the service, make the call succeed locally with realistic responses: use the app's own mock, test or offline mode if it has one; otherwise point the client at a small local stub server that start.sh also starts, or swap in a stub at the integration boundary (the API client or service module). Keep stubs out of UI code. Responses should look like what the real service returns for a real user, e.g. an AI reply that actually answers, a payment history with real-looking amounts.
- Calls the browser makes directly to outside services count too; point them at the local stub.
- For sign-in through an outside provider, create a local account or use the app's dev sign-in so you can get past it.
List every stub in app.json.

# Data: like real use
Seed it the way an established user's data would look after months of actual use: specific, plausible names and content for this kind of app; dates spread over time; a realistic mix of states (done, in progress, overdue, archived, ...); realistic volume (dozens to hundreds of records where the app revolves around records); short and long text; some messiness real data has. Start from the app's own demo or seed data if it has realistic data, and extend it if it's thin. Load data through the app's own paths (its API, import, seed scripts, or its database schema), never by hardcoding it into UI code. If the app needs an account, create one and attach the data to it. No lorem ipsum or "Test 1".

# Environment
This shell is sandboxed: you can write only inside this directory (package-manager caches already point into ./.ui-capture/cache), and the network reaches only package registries, mise's download sources and GitHub (registry.npmjs.org, registry.yarnpkg.com, repo.yarnpkg.com, github.com, codeload.github.com, objects.githubusercontent.com, raw.githubusercontent.com, nodejs.org, mise.jdx.dev, mise-versions.jdx.dev, release-assets.githubusercontent.com, pypi.org, files.pythonhosted.org, binaries.prisma.sh, cdn.jsdelivr.net, unpkg.com). Docker isn't available. A process you start in the background can't be seen or stopped from a later command, so test servers on another port than 4476 (e.g. 5476) or in the foreground under `timeout`; anything still listening on 4476 is stopped before I check.

# When you're done, leave this in ./.ui-capture/
- app.json: {"mode": "static" or "server", "entry": "/path where the main UI opens", "login": null or {"username": "...", "email": "...", "password": "..."}, "stubs": [{"service": "what was faked", "how": "how"}], "notes": "how you set it up, what data is loaded, and the main areas of the app"}
- static mode: the production build in ./.ui-capture/out, with index.html as its entry. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server; unknown paths fall back to index.html.
- server mode: ./.ui-capture/start.sh, which starts everything the app needs (stubs included) in the foreground and serves the UI at http://localhost:4476/ (it gets PORT=4476). It runs with the same PATH and restrictions as your shell, plus no network at all except localhost, so everything must already be installed, built and seeded (or seeded by start.sh itself).
- Put any scripts you write for seeding or stubbing in ./.ui-capture/ too; they're kept with the setup record.

# Order of work
You have 90 minutes in total, and anything unfinished when time runs out is lost. So work in this order:
1. Get the app building and running with its stubs, and write the contract above (app.json plus out/ or start.sh), even if it has only a little data so far.
2. Then build out the data, re-running your seed and checking the app still loads after each substantial step, so that a working state with the data loaded so far is always in place.
Write large data sets with a short generator script rather than as one long literal file.
